rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient that spans the full solvent-strength range at moderate slope and temperature, maximizing the chance that all 10 compounds elute within 42 min. This gives an initial map of retention spread, crowding, and whether later optimization should focus on weaker/stronger starts, shallower gradients, or temperature changes.

All 10 compounds are already fully resolved, so the only lever to improve CRF is reducing analysis time. A steeper full-range gradient should pull the late peak earlier while likely keeping the current minimum resolution safely above 1.5.

The 12 min gradient made the 6/7 pair under-resolved, so move slightly shallower to recover resolution while aiming to keep the run short enough to preserve the zero time penalty. This brackets the optimum between 12 and 20 min and should improve CRF if the critical pair rises above the scoring threshold.

The optimum is clearly near the current gradient length, and increasing from 14 to 16 min should selectively improve the still-critical 6/7 pair from R 1.20 toward or above 1.5 while likely keeping time penalty at zero. This is the next best local refinement before exploring temperature or composition changes.

Since 14 min is near-optimal in time but limited by one critical pair, the best chance to lift CRF is changing selectivity rather than making the gradient longer. A modest temperature decrease may improve the 6/7 separation enough to raise the resolution term while keeping the run comfortably in the zero time-penalty region.

Lowering temperature hurt selectivity, so test the opposite direction while keeping the near-optimal 14 min gradient fixed. A modest increase to 45 C may improve the crowded mid-elution cluster, especially the current 6/7 critical pair, without introducing any time penalty.

Temperature changes worsened selectivity, so keep 40 C and adjust gradient shape instead. Lowering phi1 slightly should flatten the effective gradient in the crowded mid-range and may improve the critical pair without making the run long enough to incur a meaningful time penalty.

Reducing phi1 from 0.95 to 0.90 improved the critical pair while keeping zero time penalty, so continue in the same direction. A further small decrease in phi1 should slightly weaken the gradient in the crowded region and may push the 6/7 pair to baseline resolution while still keeping the last peak comfortably early.

The best score so far came from phi1 0.90 with zero time penalty but slightly sub-threshold resolution; extending the gradient a little at that phi1 should improve the 6/7 pair without likely crossing into much time penalty. This directly tests whether phi1 0.90 can outperform both the 14 min and 0.85 endpoints.

At phi1 0.90, 14 min gave the best overall score, and 16 min incurred too much time penalty; the remaining useful bracket is 12 min. This tests whether the shorter run preserves enough of the selectivity gain from phi1 0.90 to beat the current best by cutting time further.

Gradient-end composition helped, but temperature shifts were only tested at phi1 0.95; with phi1 0.90 the selectivity landscape may differ. The best region is clearly around phi1 0.85–0.90 at 40 C, and phi1 0.85 improved resolution while 12 min shortens the run. This checks whether combining the more favorable endpoint with the shorter gradient can retain enough separation to exceed the current best score.

Endpoint tuning helped, but all critical peaks are in the crowded mid-region and the earliest peaks are still very well retained, so raising phi0 is a sensible next selectivity lever. A slightly stronger start may redistribute spacing in the central cluster and improve the limiting pair without threatening loss of the earliest compounds.

Raising phi0 improved the best CRF, and lowering phi1 previously improved the critical pair, so combining both favorable shifts is the most promising next move. This should slightly flatten the effective gradient around the crowded mid-elution zone and may push the 6/7 pair over the threshold while keeping run time near the zero-penalty boundary.

Since the maximum score is already reached, the only sensible different method is a nearby robustness check around the optimum. With a perfect score already found, the remaining value is mapping the local optimum; raising phi0 one step while keeping the winning phi1 and tG tests robustness of the start composition. This may keep full resolution while shortening the run slightly, or show that the optimum is narrow in phi0.

Two adjacent phi0 values now give the maximum CRF, so continue stepping phi0 upward at the same optimal phi1, tG, and T to define the plateau boundary. This checks whether still stronger starts preserve full resolution while further shortening retention.

Since phi0 0.15 with phi1 0.85 gives a perfect score and phi0 0.20 begins to lose the critical-pair margin, test the neighboring higher phi1 at the same phi0 to map the plateau in the other direction. The 12 min test showed 14 min is near the lower edge of the perfect-score plateau at phi0 0.15, phi1 0.85. Running 16 min maps the other side of that plateau and confirms whether the optimum is broad in gradient time or centered sharply at 14 min.

The mapped optimum appears centered at 14 min and phi0 0.10–0.15, so the remaining local dimension is whether phi1 can be lowered one more step at phi0 0.15 without losing the perfect score. This tests the lower-phi1 edge of the apparent plateau around the best method family.

A perfect score is already secured, so use the remaining runs to probe the plateau boundary near the original optimum. Testing the winning phi0/phi1 pair at a shorter tG checks whether 14 min is uniquely required there or whether the 1.000 region extends to faster methods.

The 14 min plateau is well defined, and the remaining informative corner is whether the stronger-start, lower-endpoint condition can support a shorter run. This tests if the improved critical-pair margin seen at phi0 0.15, phi1 0.80 is enough to offset the loss in resolution from moving to 12 min.

With the composition/time plateau already mapped and 40 C established as optimal for earlier conditions, the last useful dimension to probe is temperature at a perfect-score method. A small decrease tests robustness of the winning method family to temperature and whether the phi0/phi1 combination alters the temperature dependence seen in earlier nonoptimal runs.
